children: By Ben Glickman and Oyin Adedoyin
Jared Friedman discovered a way to get free credit-card points earlier this year and decided to share it with his followers on TikTok and Instagram.

After a website offering Chase Sapphire cardholders early access to World Cup tickets crashed for certain users, the bank was offering to compensate customers with 5,000 courtesy points. In his video, Friedman flagged a key detail: Chase wasn't necessarily checking whether cardholders actually tried to buy tickets.
Not long after, he said, Chase canceled two of his credit cards citing points abuse.
"I was very frustrated," said Friedman, a 33-year-old New York City resident who posts about rewards and travel to his more than 200,000 followers.
So goes the dance between a growing universe of points junkies who are constantly on the hunt for ways to milk rewards programs, and the banks that patrol for their ever-evolving tactics.

The popularity of rewards programs has created a subculture of people obsessed with maximizing their benefits, with cardholders now keeping spreadsheets and setting up calendar reminders to ensure they don't miss out on perks. But banks say some of that behavior crosses the line and violates their rules, forcing them to crack down on so-called gamers who find ways to vacuum up points, sometimes with no intention of using their cards.

Citi earlier this year implemented a policy limiting cardholders to one sign-up bonus a lifetime for its Strata cards. The rule was intended to target cardholders who try to claim bonus points by applying for the same card multiple times.

Chase implemented a similar policy last year for its Sapphire cards. The bank already had a 5/24 rule, which bans people from being approved for a new card if they have been approved for five or more from any issuers in the past 24 months — a classic sign of a gamer.

On Friday, American Express appeared to address more legitimate forms of gaming during an earnings call with analysts. Chief Executive Stephen Squeri said that while artificial intelligence may allow people "to game a little more," the technology will also make it easier to respond.
He also said the company can adjust its rules, noting Amex Platinum cardholders now need to spend $75,000 a year to bring guests into certain lounges free.

For more aggressive tactics, Amex has for years employed a team that scopes out potential abuse and claws back rewards — or axes accounts altogether. In a September job posting, the company said it was looking for a senior analyst to join its rewards integrity team, which is responsible for "detecting, mitigating and recovering losses associated with rewards leakage and benefits abuse."
Amex said it has had "longstanding efforts to protect our programs from misuse and ensure they are used as intended."

The community of gamers has thrived despite the efforts of card issuers, egged on by tips they find in online groups and from influencers. Also fueling the thirst for points: richer and richer programs, with banks increasingly competing to court big spenders with ultra-premium cards.

Rewards junkies say they are playing by the rules. But cardholder agreements generally allow banks to close an account for any reason — often with stipulations that let them seize points in such cases. Banks have also been tightening up rules for customers who might try to milk perks in less aggressive ways.
Even seasoned points mavens are running into walls.

Clint Henderson, managing editor for the rewards-card review site the Points Guy, earlier this year wanted to open a 28th credit card, and his ninth with Chase. The goal: capturing the business card's 200,000 sign-on bonus points, worth thousands of dollars.
He said he was told his application was denied because he didn't have enough business income.
"The banks have gotten wise to some of our games," Henderson said.

In New York, Friedman said he received a letter from Chase claiming his video about the World Cup ticketing snafu had provided instructions for defrauding the company. In a later video, he apologized for his actions.
"It was a learning experience at the end of the day," he said.
He didn't recover his cards, but said he was able to transfer his Chase points to other accounts.
